**Ruling:** Urborg taps for {R} only, your Dryad Arbor taps for {R} only, and your opponent's basic Island taps for {U} only. Blood Moon turns Urborg into a plain Mountain, so Urborg never makes anything a Swamp - no matter which of the two came out first.

**Why:**
1. Blood Moon: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Urborg and Dryad Arbor are nonbasic. The Island is basic, so Blood Moon doesn't touch it (CR 305.8).
2. Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type means "the land no longer has its old land type. It loses all abilities generated from its rules text ... and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type" (CR 305.7). A Mountain gets "{T}: Add {R}" (CR 305.6).
3. **Urborg** ("Each land is a Swamp in addition to its other land types") loses that ability and becomes a Mountain. It stays legendary, and its name doesn't change (Blood Moon ruling, 2020-08-07: the effect "doesn't affect names or supertypes"). It taps for {R}.
4. Timestamps don't matter here. Official Urborg ruling (2021-03-19): if an effect like Magus of the Moon makes Urborg lose its abilities by setting it to a basic land type, "it won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply." In rules terms, both are layer 4 type-changing effects (CR 613.1d), and applying Blood Moon changes whether Urborg's effect exists at all, so Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon and waits until after it (CR 613.8a-b). By then Urborg's ability is gone.
5. **Basic Island:** Blood Moon skips it, and Urborg's ability no longer exists, so it's just an Island and taps for {U} (CR 305.6).
6. **Dryad Arbor** becomes a Mountain and loses Forest, so it taps for {R} instead of {G}. Setting a land's subtype "doesn't add or remove any card types (such as creature)" (CR 305.7), and per the official ruling (2021-03-19) it "continues to be a green Dryad creature." So it's still a green 1/1 Land Creature - Mountain Dryad, and as its reminder text says, it's still "affected by summoning sickness" - you can't tap it for mana the turn it came under your control.

**Watch out for:** The Island would still be a Swamp only if Urborg's ability survived, and Blood Moon's ruling says nonbasic lands "lose any other land types and abilities they had" (2020-08-07). Blood Moon's timestamp being later or earlier doesn't save Urborg.

**Sources:** Blood Moon, Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth and Dryad Arbor (Oracle text + official rulings); CR 305.6, 305.7, 305.8, 613.1d, 613.3, 613.8a-b (CR effective September 25, 2026).

**Ruling:** No. The Helix is exiled for good. Bouncing Spell Queller before its enters trigger resolves means its leaves trigger resolves first with nothing to give back, and then the enters trigger still exiles your Helix.

**Why:**
1. The stack, bottom to top: Lightning Helix, then Queller's enters trigger ("When this creature enters, exile target spell with mana value 4 or less") targeting Helix, then your Vapor Snag.
2. Vapor Snag resolves: "Return target creature to its owner's hand. Its controller loses 1 life." Queller goes to your opponent's hand, and your opponent loses 1 life.
3. That triggers Queller's other ability: "When this creature leaves the battlefield, the exiled card's owner may cast that card without paying its mana cost." It goes on the stack above the enters trigger, so it resolves first (CR 405.5). Nothing has been exiled yet, so it does nothing.
4. Then the enters trigger resolves. It's already on the stack, so it doesn't care that Queller has left. Helix is still a legal target, so it gets exiled, and nothing is left that could let you cast it.
5. This is the exact official ruling (2025-01-24): "If Spell Queller leaves the battlefield before its 'enters' ability resolves, its leaves-the-battlefield triggered ability triggers, resolves, and does nothing. Then its first triggered ability resolves and exiles the spell forever."

**Watch out for:** Timing is everything. Let the enters trigger resolve first, and bounce Queller afterwards. Then the leaves trigger lets you cast Helix for free as it resolves, but you can't save it for later (official ruling, 2025-01-24). It's a new spell with no link to the original, so you choose its target again (same ruling date).

**Sources:** Spell Queller, Lightning Helix, Vapor Snag (Oracle text + official rulings); CR 405.5, 603.6c, 608.2b (CR effective September 25, 2026).

**Ruling:** You keep both. Spark Double's copy isn't legendary, so the legend rule never applies. And no, the copy's damage isn't commander damage: a permanent copying your commander isn't a commander, so its 21 combat damage won't make an opponent lose under the commander-damage rule.

**Why:**
1. Spark Double: "You may have this creature enter as a copy of a creature or planeswalker you control, except it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it if it's a creature ... and it isn't legendary." So it enters as a nonlegendary copy of your commander with a +1/+1 counter - a 6/6.
2. The legend rule applies only when "two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player" (CR 704.5j). Official ruling (2019-05-03): "If you control two or more permanents with the same name but only one is legendary, the 'legend rule' doesn't apply." Nothing goes to the graveyard.
3. Being a commander "is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself" (CR 903.3). Copying only copies characteristics (CR 707.2), and CR 903.3's own example says a permanent copying a commander "is not a commander."
4. The commander-damage loss needs "21 or more combat damage by the same commander" (CR 903.10a, 704.6c). The Spark Double isn't a commander, so its damage doesn't count toward that total. It's still ordinary damage and still comes off their life total.

**Watch out for:** Commander damage is tracked separately for each commander ("the same commander", CR 903.10a). Damage from the real commander and from the Spark Double copy never add together into one total.

**Sources:** Spark Double (Oracle text + official rulings); CR 704.5j, 704.6c, 707.2, 707.9b, 903.3, 903.10a (CR effective September 25, 2026).

**Ruling:** No. Ephemerate tries to return it to the battlefield without it being cast, so Containment Priest exiles it instead, and it stays in exile. It does dodge the removal, though.

**Why:**
1. Ephemerate: "Exile target creature you control, then return it to the battlefield under its owner's control."
2. Your creature is exiled. If the removal spell targeted only that creature, it's now an illegal target, so the removal won't resolve (CR 608.2b).
3. Ephemerate then tries to return the card to the battlefield. Containment Priest: "If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead." Returning it with Ephemerate isn't casting it, so that's a replacement effect (CR 614.1a). The card is exiled instead, and the event of it entering "never happens" (CR 614.6). It never touches the battlefield, so none of its enters abilities trigger.
4. It's left in exile as a new object (CR 400.7), and nothing brings it back.
5. Ephemerate itself still gets rebound if you cast it from your hand (CR 702.88a). At your next upkeep you may cast it again, but it needs a creature you control to target (official ruling, 2019-06-14).

**Watch out for:** Containment Priest only stops something entering *as a creature*. Official ruling (2021-03-19): a creature card that wasn't cast but enters as a noncreature permanent (for example Heliod, Sun-Crowned without enough devotion) isn't exiled. That only matters if your creature is something like that, which isn't in the question.

**Sources:** Containment Priest, Ephemerate (Oracle text + official rulings); CR 400.7, 608.2b, 614.1a, 614.6, 702.88a (CR effective September 25, 2026).

**Ruling:** No ordering, no lethal-first requirement. You divide your 5 damage however you like between the two blockers, so yes, you can put all 5 on the 4/4.

**Why:**
1. CR 510.1c: "If two or more creatures are blocking it, it assigns its combat damage to those creatures divided as its controller chooses among them." Its example has a 4/3 blocked by a 2/3 and a 1/1 that can put "all 4 damage to the Hunter" or any other split.
2. Damage assignment order no longer exists. The CR glossary lists "Damage Assignment Order" as obsolete: the controller "simply divides its combat damage as they choose among all creatures it's blocking or blocked by" (see CR 510.1c-d).
3. All 5 on the 4/4 is lethal for it. The 2/2 takes nothing. At the same time, the blockers assign their damage to your 5/5 (CR 510.1d), and all combat damage is dealt simultaneously (CR 510.2). 2 + 4 = 6, so with no other effects your 5/5 dies too.

**Watch out for:** Trample is different. A trampler must assign lethal damage to all its blockers before any excess can go to the player (CR 702.19b). That only comes up if your creature has trample, which isn't in the question.

**Sources:** CR 510.1, 510.1c, 510.1d, 510.2, 702.19b; glossary "Damage Assignment Order (Obsolete)" (CR effective September 25, 2026).

**Ruling:** After Twisted Image it's a 4/3; after Giant Growth it's a 7/6. If Bonesplitter then moves to another creature, it becomes a 7/4.

**Why:** The switch is always applied last, after every other power/toughness effect, no matter when those effects started.
1. Twisted Image: "Switch target creature's power and toughness until end of turn." Bonesplitter: "Equipped creature gets +2/+0."
2. Layer 7c holds the modifiers (Bonesplitter's +2/+0, later Giant Growth's +3/+3); layer 7d holds the switch (CR 613.4c, 613.4d).
3. Before Giant Growth: 1/4 + 2/0 = 3/4, then switch = **4/3**.
4. After Giant Growth ("Target creature gets +3/+3 until end of turn"): 1/4 + 2/0 + 3/3 = 6/7, then switch = **7/6**. Official Twisted Image ruling (2021-03-19): "Effects that switch a creature's power and toughness apply after all other effects, regardless of when those effects began to apply." CR 613.4d's example works the same way.
5. Bonesplitter moves away: its +2/+0 no longer applies, so 1/4 + 3/3 = 4/7, then switch = **7/4**. (CR 613.4d example: if a modifier stops applying before the switch ends, recompute and switch again.)

**Watch out for:** Damage marked this turn stays on it, so a switch or losing the Equipment can turn nonlethal damage lethal (Twisted Image ruling, 2021-03-19). At 7/4, it dies if it has 4 or more damage marked.

**Sources:** Bonesplitter, Twisted Image (rulings 2021-03-19), Giant Growth; CR 613.1, 613.4c, 613.4d, 613.7. CR effective September 25, 2026.

**Ruling:** No. Split second doesn't stop triggered abilities. Krosan Grip has mana value 3, so Chalice triggers, its trigger resolves first, and Krosan Grip is countered. The Chalice survives.

**Why:**
1. Krosan Grip ({2}{G}, mana value 3) is cast. Chalice: "Whenever a player casts a spell with mana value equal to the number of charge counters on this artifact, counter that spell." With 3 counters, that triggers.
2. Split second only stops players from casting spells and activating non-mana abilities (CR 702.61a). CR 702.61b: "Triggered abilities trigger and are put on the stack as normal while a spell with split second is on the stack." Triggered abilities aren't cast or activated, so they work even when casting and activating aren't allowed (CR 603.2a).
3. The Chalice trigger goes on the stack above Krosan Grip and resolves first, countering it. Krosan Grip never resolves, so nothing gets destroyed.
4. Official Krosan Grip ruling (2021-03-19): "Split second doesn't stop triggered abilities from triggering, such as that of Chalice of the Void."

**Watch out for:** The count is checked only when the spell is cast. Removing a counter from Chalice afterward doesn't save Krosan Grip, and getting rid of Chalice once it has triggered doesn't either (Chalice rulings, 2021-03-19). Split second also stops you casting anything in response to the trigger.

**Sources:** Chalice of the Void (rulings 2021-03-19), Krosan Grip (rulings 2021-03-19); CR 603.2, 603.2a, 702.61a, 702.61b. CR effective September 25, 2026.

**Ruling:** All three are enchantment creatures with no abilities. Humility is 4/4, the first Opalescence is 4/4, and the second Opalescence is 1/1.

**Why:** An official ruling covers this exact order. Opalescence/Humility ruling (2006-02-01): "If the timestamp order is Opalescence, Humility, Opalescence, the second Opalescence is 1/1, and the Humility and first Opalescence are 4/4." Here's how the layers produce that:
1. Layer 4 (type, CR 613.1d): Opalescence: "Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types and has base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value." Opalescence #1 animates Humility and Opalescence #2. Opalescence #2 animates Humility and Opalescence #1. All three are now creatures.
2. Layer 6 (abilities, CR 613.1f): Humility: "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." All three, Humility included, lose their abilities.
3. Losing an ability in layer 6 doesn't stop effects that already started in layer 4. Once an effect starts applying, it keeps applying in its later layers (CR 613.6). The 2009-10-01 ruling says the same: "The rest of it will apply even if the permanent loses its ability before it's finished applying."
4. Layer 7b (setting base P/T, CR 613.4b), in timestamp order (CR 613.7): Opalescence #1 makes Humility and Opalescence #2 4/4 (each costs {2}{W}{W}, mana value 4). Then Humility makes all three 1/1. Then Opalescence #2 makes Humility and Opalescence #1 4/4 again.
5. Opalescence #2 never affects itself ("each *other*"), so Humility's 1/1 is the last thing applied to it.

**Watch out for:** The order is the whole answer. With Humility last, everything is 1/1; with Humility first, everything is 4/4 (same 2006-02-01 ruling). There's no dependency between Humility and Opalescence here, because their effects don't conflict in the same layer (CR 613.8a), so timestamps decide.

**Sources:** Opalescence, Humility (rulings 2006-02-01, 2009-10-01); CR 613.1d, 613.1f, 613.4b, 613.6, 613.7, 613.8a. CR effective September 25, 2026.

**Ruling:** Nothing changes. Urborg is a nonbasic land too, so Blood Moon makes it a Mountain with no Urborg ability, and it can't make anything a Swamp. Your Dryad Arbor is still just a Mountain (1/1 green Dryad creature) that taps only for {R}, whichever one came down first.

**Why:**
1. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a "Legendary Land", not a basic one, so Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") applies to it.
2. Both effects are type-changing effects in layer 4 (CR 613.1d). Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's: applying Blood Moon removes Urborg's ability, which changes whether Urborg's effect exists (CR 613.8a). A dependent effect waits until after the effect it depends on (CR 613.8b), and dependency overrides timestamps (CR 613.8). So Blood Moon applies first.
3. Once Urborg is set to Mountain, it "loses all abilities generated from its rules text" (CR 305.7). That includes "Each land is a Swamp in addition to its other land types", so no land becomes a Swamp.
4. Official Urborg ruling (2021-03-19): "If an effect such as that of Magus of the Moon causes Urborg to lose its abilities by setting it to a basic land type not in addition to its other types, it won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply." Blood Moon does the same thing.
5. Dryad Arbor is still covered as before: Blood Moon makes it a Mountain, it taps for {R}, and it keeps its creature type and Dryad subtype (CR 305.7; Dryad Arbor ruling 2021-03-19: "If Dryad Arbor is changed into another basic land type, it continues to be a green Dryad creature.").

**Watch out for:** Players often expect Urborg to win if it came down after Blood Moon. Timestamps don't matter here because of the dependency. If Blood Moon leaves the battlefield, Urborg works again and Dryad Arbor goes back to being a Forest that is also a Swamp.

**Sources:** Blood Moon, Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth (rulings 2021-03-19), Dryad Arbor (rulings 2021-03-19); CR 305.7, 613.1d, 613.3, 613.8, 613.8a, 613.8b. CR effective September 25, 2026.

**Ruling:** Your Clone becomes a face-up, colorless 2/2 creature with no name, no subtypes, no abilities and no mana cost. You can't pay the morph cost to turn it "face up". It's already face up and has no morph ability.

**Why:**
1. Clone: "You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield." A copy gets the original's copiable values, "as modified by... its face-down status" (CR 707.2).
2. A face-down morph's copiable values are only what the face-down rules give it: a 2/2 creature with no text, no name, no subtypes and no mana cost (CR 702.37c, 708.2, 708.2a). That's all Clone copies. It doesn't get the hidden card's name, abilities or morph cost.
3. Clone doesn't copy the face-down status itself (status isn't copied, CR 707.2), so the Clone is face up.
4. Turning a permanent face up with morph means paying its morph cost, and if the permanent "wouldn't have a morph cost if it were face up, it can't be turned face up this way" (CR 702.37e). Your Clone has no morph ability.
5. CR 707.2 has this exact example: Clone copying a face-down Grinning Demon "is a colorless 2/2 creature with no name, no types, no abilities, and no mana cost. It will still be face up. Its controller can't pay {2}{B}{B} to turn it face up."

**Watch out for:** If your opponent later turns their morph face up, your Clone stays a blank 2/2. Changing the original's copiable values after it's been copied doesn't change the copy (CR 707.2b). You also don't get to look at the face-down card.

**Sources:** Clone (rulings 2025-10-02); CR 702.37c, 702.37e, 707.2, 707.2b, 708.2, 708.2a. CR effective September 25, 2026.
